h1: The 5 Best Microphone Arms for Podcasting of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Mic Arms for Podcasting: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 5 microphone arms for podcasting scored on mic fit, cable routing, clamp design and profile, from under $25 up.
summary: The Shure by Gator Deluxe Broadcast arm is our top pick for serious podcasters because its threaded extension adapter clears XLR cables and it is designed around vocal mics. The FIFINE BM88 is the better value, with a low profile and built-in cable management. The InnoGear is the cheapest dependable choice for Blue Yeti-class mics, and the KRISKUL fits only lightweight mics.
intro: Podcasters usually blame the microphone for bad audio when the real culprit is the way it is held. A mic on a desk stand picks up every keyboard tap, elbow bump and coffee cup set down, because the desk carries those vibrations straight into the capsule. An arm lifts the microphone off the desk and puts it where your mouth is, which cuts desk noise and lets you speak at a steady distance.

We ranked five arms by reading the listings for what actually matters on a recording desk: what weight and mic type each is built for, how the cable is handled, how the clamp attaches and how much the arm intrudes into your field of view. The spec detail varies a lot between listings, so we scored cautiously where a number was missing.

products.name: Shure by Gator Deluxe Broadcast Desktop Mic Boom Arm (SH-BROADCAST1)
products.verdict: A broadcast-style arm built around vocal mics, with an extension adapter that clears XLR cables.
products.description:
The SH-BROADCAST1 is designed to hold Shure and other-brand vocal microphones, clamps to any desk, table or similar-sized surface, and includes a threaded extension adapter that gives XLR connectors room to clear the mount.

It ranks first because that adapter solves a real podcasting annoyance: a straight XLR plug can foul on the arm and kink the cable, adding handling noise. None of the cheaper arms here list an equivalent. It also belongs to the broadcast category, built around professional dynamic mics rather than gaming condensers.

Buy it for an XLR dynamic mic on a permanent desk. The drawback is that it sells in the $100 to $200 range with no weight rating listed, so check your mic against the listing before you order.
pros: Clamps to any desk or table
cons: More arm than USB mics need
products.idealFor: XLR dynamic mics on a permanent podcasting desk.
products.skipIf: You use a light USB mic and want the lowest price.

products.name: FIFINE BM88 Low Profile Microphone Boom Arm Stand for Gaming Streaming
products.verdict: A sturdy metal low-profile arm with cable management for the price of a lunch out.
products.description:
The FIFINE BM88 is a sturdy metal arm with a low profile and built-in cable management. Low profile means the arm sits close to the desk and swings out of your line of sight, so it does not block your monitor or camera.

It ranks second to the Shure because the Shure is aimed at XLR vocal mics and adds a cable-clearance adapter, while the BM88 is pitched at gaming and streaming setups. It is a better design than the cheaper arms below, with its built-in cable routing keeping the lead from dangling across the desk.

Pick it for a USB or XLR mic on a tidy desk. The caveat is the $50 to $100 bucket with no weight rating listed, so confirm your mic's weight.
pros: Low profile stays out of view
products.idealFor: Desks where the arm must stay out of the camera frame.
products.skipIf: You want a vocal-mic adapter or the lowest price.

products.name: InnoGear Boom Arm Microphone Mic Stand for Blue Yeti Fifine HyperX
products.verdict: A heavy-duty free-position arm named for popular USB mics, at the lowest price tier.
products.description:
InnoGear is a free-position mic arm described as solid and heavy-duty, with a name that points at Blue Yeti, Fifine and HyperX microphones. The under $25 price is its main draw.

It ranks third because the listing offers little hardware detail: no weight rating, no clamp spec. The FIFINE BM88 gives you a stated low profile and cable management for the next price step, while this is the arm to buy when the budget is the constraint.

Choose it for a USB mic on a home podcast desk. The caveat is the missing specs, so match your mic against the model names in the title.
products.idealFor: USB mics on a budget home podcasting desk.
products.skipIf: You need cable routing or a documented weight limit.

products.name: QuadCast Boom Arm
products.verdict: A spring-supported boom arm with dual suspension springs, for a mic that fits its design.
products.description:
The QuadCast Boom Arm is listed as a mic boom arm with dual suspension springs, sold in the under $25 bucket. Springs inside the arm counter the weight of the mic so it floats in place and moves smoothly.

It ranks fourth because the listing gives no weight rating or mount details, and its name points at one microphone family. It is cheaper than the BM88, but the BM88 documents cable management and a low profile that this listing does not.

Buy it if you use the mic the arm is named after, since that pairing is the one the maker designed around. The caveat is compatibility: confirm the mount thread and the weight before trusting it with a different microphone, because a mismatch shows up as a slow sag mid-episode.
products.idealFor: Owners of the QuadCast-style mic the arm is named for.
products.skipIf: You use a different mic and want documented compatibility.

products.name: KRISKUL Low Profile Mic Arm for Lightweight Mics
products.verdict: A low-profile arm with a metal ball head and heavy-duty clamp, limited to lightweight mics.
products.description:
KRISKUL is a low-profile arm with smooth adjustment, a heavy-duty desk clamp and an upgraded all-metal ball head. The ball head holds the mic angle firmly after you set it.

It ranks last because the title says it is for lightweight mics, which rules out heavier dynamic mics common in podcasting. Against the InnoGear it offers a clearer clamp spec and a metal head, but narrower compatibility.

Buy it for a small, light condenser or lavalier-style mic. The caveat is that anything heavy will sag, so do not pair it with a large dynamic microphone.
products.idealFor: Small, light microphones on a tidy desk.
products.skipIf: You use a heavy dynamic or large condenser mic.

whatMatters.detail: Boom arms hold a limited weight, and a mic that is too heavy makes the arm droop after a few minutes. Dynamic broadcast mics are heavier than USB condensers. Look for a rated weight range on the listing and compare it to your mic including its shock mount and pop filter, and be wary of arms that state only a brand name and give no figure.

A loose cable swinging off the arm adds handling noise, and a straight XLR plug can foul on the arm. Built-in channels or clips route the lead along the arm. Look for named cable clips, and for the Shure's threaded extension adapter, which moves the connector clear of the arm so the cable hangs free.

A desk clamp must grip firmly without marking the surface or wobbling when you lean on the desk. Check the maximum desk thickness it accepts and whether the clamp pads are protected. A loose clamp transmits desk vibration straight into the microphone, which defeats the purpose of using an arm, so tighten it fully and test it by bumping the desk.

A low-profile arm sits near the desk and stays out of your camera frame, while a tall arm gives more reach but can block sightlines. Podcasters on video should favor low-profile designs. Check the listing photos for how far the arm rises, and place the pivot point so the mic sits just below your chin.

Internal springs balance the weight of the mic so it stays where you put it, but springs can lose tension over time and let the arm drift. Dual spring arms balance heavier loads more evenly. Look for adjustable tension, and tighten the joints after setup to stop a slow downward sag. If you swap to a heavier microphone later, retension the arm again.

faq.q: Will these arms fit my USB mic?
faq.a: Most arms use a standard thread, but check your mic's weight against the listing. The InnoGear names Blue Yeti, Fifine and HyperX mics, while the KRISKUL is limited to lightweight mics. If the weight is not listed, ask the seller.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with a mic arm?
faq.a: Mounting the mic too far from the mouth. An arm lets you hold a steady distance, but the Shure by Gator or FIFINE BM88 only helps if you position it a hand's width from your lips and slightly off-axis.

faq.q: Is an arm worth it over a desk stand?
faq.a: For podcasting, yes. A desk stand carries keyboard and table vibration into the mic, while the Shure or BM88 clamp lifts the mic off the desk. The InnoGear adds that benefit under $25.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Clamp the base to the desk edge, screw the mic mount on, route the cable along the arm with clips and set the tension. On the Shure, fit the extension adapter first so the XLR plug clears the mount.

faq.q: How do I stop the arm drooping?
faq.a: Tighten each joint and check the mic is within the arm's weight rating. Spring arms such as the QuadCast Boom Arm can lose tension over time. If it still sags, the mic is likely too heavy for that arm.

faq.q: Can I use an arm with a shock mount?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. The shock mount threads onto the arm end, then the mic sits in the mount. The Shure by Gator is designed for vocal mics, but check thread size on the other arms before buying a separate shock mount.

finalTake: Buy the Shure by Gator Deluxe Broadcast arm if you record on an XLR dynamic mic: the extension adapter and broadcast build suit the job. The FIFINE BM88 is the smarter buy for most home podcasters, with low profile and cable routing at a mid price. Pick the InnoGear when budget rules, and keep the KRISKUL for small lightweight mics only.
